title: SYSK Selects: How Pollen Works
summary: A Stuff You Should Know "Selects" rerun of a July episode on how pollen works. The hosts open with small talk about pollen counts in Atlanta, then cover pollen's evolutionary history (gymnosperms and angiosperms), the shapes and functions of pollen grains, plant reproductive parts (pistil, stigma, style, ovary, stamen, anther, filament), self- versus cross-pollination and plant mechanisms that prevent self-pollination, pine cone reproduction and naked seeds, flower adaptations that attract pollinators (bees, birds, bats, beetles), the Devil's Tongue and philodendron stink-pollination, and the debate over pollen drift from GMO crops and patents. A listener-mail segment corrects a mix-up between the drugs propranolol and propofol from an earlier PTSD episode. The episode ends with a plug for the how allergies work episode and the show's sign-off.

segments.title: Opening banter and Selects introduction
segments.summary: Josh introduces this Selects episode from July, explaining it is about pollen during pollen season. The hosts joke about pollen counts in Atlanta and the yellow streets during pollen season.

segments.title: Pollen's history and food crops
segments.summary: The hosts note that about a third of the plants people eat depend on pollination, and discuss bananas as sterile clones propagated by humans. They describe pollen's evolutionary origin about 375 million years ago, with gymnosperms first, and why pollen evolved so plants did not depend on water to carry their reproductive material.

segments.title: What pollen looks like and why shapes matter
segments.summary: Pollen grains vary widely in shape, from blowfish-like to starfish-like, with some having wings for wind dispersal, such as dandelion pollen. The hosts mention phytonutrients in bitter plants like dandelion greens and how people bred bitter compounds out of food over time.

segments.title: Flower anatomy and self-pollinating dandelions
segments.summary: The hosts describe the female parts (pistil, ovary, style, stigma) and male parts (filament, anther) of flowers. They distinguish gymnosperms (naked seed) from angiosperms and explain self-pollination, cross-pollination, and how dandelions curl back to pollinate themselves.

segments.title: Mechanisms that prevent self-pollination
segments.summary: The hosts discuss why many plants avoid self-pollination and how a wider gene pool helps. They cite peanuts as self-pollinators and corn as using timing differences to force cross-pollination, and describe separate male and female plants and biochemical blocks.

segments.title: Pine cones, naked seeds, and angiosperm fruit
segments.summary: The hosts walk through pine reproduction: pollen lands on the sticky female cone, forms a pollen tube, and fertilizes the ovule, which becomes a naked seed. They contrast this with angiosperms, which flower and protect seeds in fruit, and discuss how fruit-eating animals spread seeds.

segments.title: Flower adaptations, pollinators, and smelly flowers
segments.summary: The hosts discuss flowers shaped and colored to attract specific pollinators such as bumblebees and foxglove, and nectar as a lure. They describe the Devil's Tongue flower, which smells like decaying flesh to attract carrion beetles, and the philodendron's heat-generated odor.

segments.title: Pollen grains, meiosis, and endosperm
segments.summary: The hosts explain how pollen grains form through meiosis in pollen sacks on the anther and carry sperm cells. In angiosperms, two sperm are used, with one fertilizing the egg and the other forming endosperm, the starchy food that corn kernels contain.

segments.title: GMO crops, pollen drift, and patents
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the conflict where pollen from genetically modified crops can drift to neighboring farms, including organic farms, raising patent infringement concerns. They mention distance and crop rotation timing as ways to reduce cross-pollination, and give their opinion that living organisms should not be patented.

segments.title: Message break
segments.summary: A short break in the episode.

segments.title: Listener correction: propranolol vs. propofol
segments.summary: A listener named Chris corrects an earlier PTSD episode where the hosts confused propranolol, a mild beta blocker, with propofol, a powerful intravenous anesthetic linked to Michael Jackson's death. He notes propofol has a steep dose-response curve and high overdose risk.

segments.title: Outro and pointers
segments.summary: The hosts recommend the How Allergies Work episode for how pollen causes allergies, invite corrections and feedback through social media and email, and sign off.
